title: g-force, m/s², ft/s² and the gal: Acceleration Units
h1: g-force is an acceleration — m/s², ft/s² and the galileo
description: 1 g = 9.80665 m/s² exactly = 32.174 ft/s² = 980.665 Gal. Standard gravity, the gal gravimeters print, and why an accelerometer at rest already reads about 1 g.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 (standard gravity), the 3rd CGPM (1901) value of gₙ, and the 1959 international foot

hero: One g is not a force. It is exactly 9.80665 metres per second squared — 32.174 feet per second squared, or 980.665 gal. An accelerometer sitting still on a desk already reads about 1 g.
body: Acceleration is the change of velocity per unit time. The SI unit is the metre per second squared (m/s²). Everything else that shows up in workshops, cockpits and gravity surveys — the g, the foot per second squared, and the gal — is a fixed multiple of that unit. The trap is the name. 'g-force' sounds like a force. It is an acceleration, equal to the conventional standard acceleration of free fall. Force comes later, when you multiply by mass.

> 1 g = gₙ = 9.80665 m/s² (exact, standard gravity)
> 1 ft/s² = 0.3048 m/s² (exact, international foot)
> 1 g = 32.1740486 ft/s²
> 1 Gal = 1 cm/s² = 0.01 m/s² (exact)
> 1 g = 980.665 Gal
> 1 mGal = 10⁻⁵ m/s²

Standard gravity gₙ was fixed at 9.80665 m/s² by the 3rd General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1901, and NIST SP 811 still uses that exact value when it converts kilogram-force and pound-force. It is not the gravity at your latitude. On the GRS80 reference ellipsoid, normal gravity is about 9.780 m/s² at the equator and about 9.832 m/s² at the poles — a swing of roughly half a percent. A spring scale or an accelerometer follows local g. A conversion that quotes 'g' almost always means the conventional 9.80665, not whatever the instrument felt that morning.

The international foot has been 0.3048 m exactly since the 1959 agreement between the English-speaking countries. Dividing standard gravity by that foot gives 32.1740486 ft/s². Rounding to 32.2 ft/s² is fine for a braking estimate and wrong for a dynamics answer that is graded to four figures. The older US survey foot (1200/3937 m) was deprecated for most work at the end of 2022; it does not belong in an ft/s² conversion.
## The gal, the unit gravimeters actually print

The galileo (symbol Gal, capital G, so nobody confuses it with the gallon) is one centimetre per second squared. It is not an SI unit, but geodesy never dropped it: a relative gravity meter reports anomalies in milligals. Standard gravity is exactly 980.665 Gal, because 9.80665 m/s² divided by 0.01 m/s² is 980.665. One milligal is 10⁻⁵ m/s², about one part in a million of g. The free-air gradient is about 0.3086 mGal for each metre of elevation, so a 10 m staircase changes measured g by roughly 3 mGal. A phone accelerometer cannot see that. A mineral survey is built out of it.

Metres per second squared belong in SI dynamics, in vehicle specifications written to ISO, and in any calculation you intend to multiply by a mass in kilograms to get newtons. Feet per second squared survive in US aerospace notes and older flight-test reports; the same 1 g is 32.174 ft/s². The bare 'g' is the cockpit unit and the roller-coaster unit. A dry-pavement emergency stop in a modern passenger car is often 0.8–1.0 g. Many steel coasters briefly reach 3.5–4.5 g. A fighter designed for a sustained +9 g is asking the pilot to tolerate 88.3 m/s², which is 9 × 9.80665. The gal stays inside gravimetry. It does not belong on a wrench, a tyre placard, or a car brochure.
## What an accelerometer is actually reading

Proper acceleration is what a scale or an accelerometer reports. Leave the sensor on a desk and it reads about +1 g upward — the desk pushing back — not zero. Drop it and, once it is in free fall, the reading falls toward 0 g, even though its speed toward the ground is changing at nearly 9.8 m/s². Coordinate acceleration (the dv/dt a textbook problem asks for) and proper acceleration (the number on the instrument) differ by local gravity. Mixing them is how a 1 g braking specification gets double-counted as 2 g, and how a 'zero-g' flight is described as having no acceleration when the aeroplane is simply following a ballistic arc.

A car stops from 100 km/h at a steady 0.8 g on dry pavement. Convert the acceleration before the distance. 0.8 × 9.80665 = 7.845 m/s². The same figure is 0.8 × 32.174 = 25.74 ft/s², or 784.5 Gal. Speed is 100 / 3.6 = 27.778 m/s. Braking distance, with reaction time left out, is v² / (2a) = 771.6 / 15.69 = 49.2 m, which is 161 ft. Swap 32.174 for the rounded 32.2 and the foot-per-second-squared result moves by less than a tenth of a percent. Replace 9.80665 with a flat 10 and the stopping distance comes out about 2% short. That is the size of the error hiding in 'just use 10'.

Divide a force in newtons by a mass in kilograms and you are back in m/s². Under standard gravity a 1 kg mass weighs 9.80665 N, which is why a bathroom scale can print '1 kg' after it has measured about 9.81 N and divided by gₙ. The kilogram-force and the pound-force are forces defined by multiplying a mass by this same standard gravity. They are not acceleration units. If a drawing says '5 g shock', it means an acceleration of 5 × 9.80665 m/s², and the force on a bracket is that acceleration times the bracket's mass. The hinge between the two families of units is the single number 9.80665.
1 g = 9.80665 m/s² = 32.174 ft/s² = 980.665 Gal. g is an acceleration, not a force. An accelerometer at rest reads about 1 g. Gravimeters speak milligals, and one milligal is 10⁻⁵ m/s².

faqs.a: Neither, when you need the defined constant. Standard gravity gₙ is 9.80665 m/s² exactly. 9.81 is a three-figure rounding. 9.8 is fine for a sketch and about 0.07% low.

faqs.q: Why does my phone show 1 g when I am not moving?
faqs.a: The accelerometer measures proper acceleration — the contact force from the desk or your hand — not coordinate acceleration. At rest that contact force balances weight, so the reading is about 1 g. In free fall it falls toward 0 g.

faqs.q: Is a gal the same as a gallon?
faqs.a: No. The galileo, symbol Gal, is an acceleration of 0.01 m/s². A US gallon is a volume. The capital G in Gal is there so the two are not swapped in a sentence.

faqs.q: How many ft/s² are in one g?
faqs.a: 32.1740486 ft/s², from 9.80665 divided by 0.3048. The textbook shortcut 32.2 ft/s² is within 0.1%.

faqs.q: What is a milligal in everyday terms?
faqs.a: 1 mGal = 10⁻⁵ m/s², about one millionth of standard gravity. Ten metres of extra elevation changes gravity by roughly 3 mGal. A phone cannot resolve it. A relative gravimeter can.
